pdf_title: Multi-Sensor NDVI-Based FVC Retrieval Agreement with Copernicus FCOVER on a Common 300 m Support: Geographic Heterogeneity and Historical-Window Transfer across Qinghai Plateau AOIs
accuracy_occurrences: Native-resolution sensor comparisons with 300 m FCOVER can conflate retrieval behavior with spatial-support mismatch, while geographic and historical transfer remain uncertain. The methodological contribution is an integrated evaluation framework combining exact common-support harmonization, environmentally contrasting AOI replication, spatially blocked diagnostics, and chronological forward-transfer testing of historical training depth. We evaluated Sentinel-2, Landsat 8/9, and MODIS NDVI-based FVC retrievals against Copernicus FCOVER during 2021--2025 using three summer dates, four frozen Qinghai plateau AOIs, 5 km blocks, six historical windows, and 2024/2025 Rolling-Origin targets. All 144 formal runs were complete. Multi-AOI descriptive mean RMSE was 0.041023 for Sentinel-2, 0.036840 for Landsat, and 0.030787 for MODIS; no cross-sensor inferential ranking was performed. AOI mean RMSE ranged from 0.00139 to 0.05674, preferred windows and fitted coefficients varied with domain and historical composition, and spatial-fold coefficient dispersion provided a second stability diagnostic. Only 12 of 24 sensor--AOI--target trajectories were monotonic or non-degrading; 12 were non-monotonic. Across 24 predefined sensor--AOI--target families, Holm correction was applied separately to three historical-depth contrasts per family; 40 of 72 contrasts met the within-family adjusted significance criterion, including 32 favoring longer history and eight indicating degradation. Eleven significant AOI-01 effects had $|\Delta\mathrm{RMSE}|<0.0001$. Common-support harmonization makes product-reference comparisons structurally consistent but does not remove geographic, coefficient, or temporal heterogeneity; historical training depth must therefore be validated for the intended target domain rather than assumed to improve forward transfer. These findings concern agreement with Copernicus FCOVER as an operational reference and do not establish absolute field-level FVC accuracy.

Copernicus FCOVER is an operational satellite-product reference, not field ground truth; its algorithm, compositing, and inherited uncertainty remain part of the comparison \cite{baret2013,camacho2013,fuster2020,copernicus2025validation}. The study evaluates FCOVER-reference agreement on the common 300 m support and does not establish native-resolution or absolute field-level FVC accuracy. Independent field, UAV, or validated high-resolution references and probability-based sampling would be required for that claim \cite{mu2015sampling,chen2016uav,olofsson2014}.

Common-support harmonization enabled controlled evaluation of sensor-specific NDVI-based FVC retrievals against Copernicus FCOVER. For RQ1, historically calibrated OLS produced substantially lower AOI-00 reference error than the tested endpoint settings under their distinct information conditions; sensor differences on the 300 m support remain descriptive and do not imply absolute field-level FVC accuracy. For RQ2, geographic error heterogeneity was large, preferred windows varied by sensor and AOI, full-fit slopes and intercepts changed with historical composition, and GroupKFold coefficient dispersion reinforced that coefficient behavior is conditional rather than spatially invariant. These descriptive diagnostics do not establish statistically different coefficients or a causal mechanism.

For RQ3, only 12 of 24 forward trajectories were monotonic or non-degrading. Longer history could improve or degrade FCOVER-reference agreement: within the 24 separately corrected three-contrast families, 32 effects favored longer history and eight favored shorter history, while several AOI-01 effects were statistically detectable but practically tiny. Historical composition should therefore be selected using spatial stability and pseudo-future temporal transfer for the intended domain, with effect magnitude reported alongside within-family adjusted $p$ values, rather than by assuming that more historical observations are inherently preferable. These conclusions concern agreement with Copernicus FCOVER and do not establish absolute field-level FVC accuracy.

The study asks: \textbf{RQ1.} After harmonization to the native 300 m Copernicus FCOVER support, what level of FCOVER-reference agreement is achieved by sensor-specific NDVI-based FVC retrievals, and, in the AOI-00 comparator, how does historically calibrated OLS compare with formula-based endpoint retrieval under its distinct information condition? \textbf{RQ2.} How stable are FCOVER-reference error, fitted OLS coefficients, and preferred historical windows across sensors, AOIs, and historical compositions, and does a single historical window provide geographically invariant behavior? \textbf{RQ3.} Under chronological forward evaluation to 2024 and 2025, does increasing historical training depth consistently improve FCOVER-reference agreement, and what are the direction, magnitude, and within-family statistical support of the resulting block-level differences? Cross-sensor comparisons are descriptive, and all conclusions concern FCOVER-reference agreement rather than absolute field-level FVC accuracy.
